subject: Astronomy & Space
title: The Sun: Our Nearest Star
description: A 60-second lesson on The Sun: Our Nearest Star.

hook.text: The Sun holds 99.86% of all mass in the solar system. Every planet and moon is a tiny leftover.

buildup.text: It's a yellow dwarf, 4.6 billion years old. Its core fuses hydrogen into helium at 15 million °C.

discovery.text: Each second, 600 million tons of hydrogen become helium. The lost mass converts to energy via E=mc².

twist.text: A photon born at the core takes 100,000 years to reach the surface—then only 8 minutes to hit Earth.

climax.text: In 5 billion years, the Sun will swell into a red giant, consuming Mercury and Venus.

punchline.text: One ordinary star. It runs everything we know.

quiz.question: How long does it take a photon to travel from the Sun's core to its surface?

details.summary: The Sun is a G-type main-sequence star containing 99.86% of the solar system's total mass. Its core fuses 600 million tons of hydrogen into helium every second at 15 million degrees Celsius, producing the energy that powers all life on Earth.
details.whyItMatters: The Sun is the engine that drives Earth's climate, weather, and biology. Understanding it helps predict space weather, protect satellites and power grids, and appreciate how rare stable, long-lived stars — and habitable planets — truly are.
takeaways: The Sun contains 99.86% of the solar system's mass
Its core fuses 600 million tons of hydrogen per second
It's 4.6 billion years old with about 5 billion years remaining

faq.question: How does the Sun produce energy?
faq.answer: Through nuclear fusion in its core, where extreme temperature and pressure force hydrogen nuclei together into helium. Each reaction converts a tiny amount of mass into energy (E=mc²). The Sun converts about 4 million tons of mass into energy every second, radiating it as light and heat.

faq.question: How long does sunlight take to reach Earth?
faq.answer: About 8 minutes and 20 seconds to cross the 150-million-kilometer gap. However, the photons produced in the Sun's core take roughly 100,000 years to fight through the dense interior to the surface — then just 8 minutes across empty space to reach your eyes.
